title: A softening labor market narrows mobility while AI access and control remain stratified
source_unit: Federal Reserve Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking adult respondent, 2025; employment, job-movement, schedule, and generative-AI tables

observations.period: 2023 to 2025; difficulty finding work among adults ages 18 to 29

denominator.unit: published percentage base among adults ages 18 to 29; reason categories can coexist

total_difficulty_finding_work_2025.unit: percent of adults ages 18 to 29; sum of two reported categories, not a unique-person estimate

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published age-specific reason-for-not-working and part-time-for-no-full-time estimates; the two reasons are retained as separate measures.
observations.uncertainty: The cross-sectional survey does not identify duration, prior work history, search intensity, local labor demand, household support, or whether the categories overlap beyond the report's combined presentation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Not working or working part time may reflect schooling, health, care, preference, or another reason; difficulty finding work is a reported contribution, not a complete causal account.

observations.period: 2022 to 2025; layoffs, voluntary exits, and job changes among adults

denominator.unit: published percentage bases among all adults; indicators are separate populations/events

started_new_job_2022.unit: percent of adults; peak reported in comparison

new_job_better_2025.unit: percent of adults who changed jobs and answered the comparison item

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published annual job-separation and job-movement comparisons; layoffs, voluntary exits, new jobs, and perceived improvement retain separate denominators.
observations.uncertainty: These are retrospective self-reports with changing question comparability before 2020; they do not measure employer-level layoffs, job duration, wages, benefits, or the reasons for each move.
observations.subgroup: All adults, with a reported Black-adult layoff subgroup and job changers for the improvement measure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower voluntary exits can reflect job satisfaction, fewer attractive alternatives, or both; a job described as better does not establish durable security or bargaining power.

observations.period: 2025 SHED; generative-AI use, perceived benefits, and replacement concern among workers

denominator.unit: published percentage base among workers; use and attitude items have distinct response wording

ai_saves_time_all_workers.unit: percent of workers agreeing generative AI saves time in their job

ai_improves_quality_all_workers.unit: percent of workers who used generative AI agreeing it improved quality

ai_use_high_school_or_less.unit: percent of workers with high school degree or less

ai_use_graduate_degree.unit: percent of workers with a graduate degree

ai_use_high_task_control.unit: percent of employees often or always controlling how to complete tasks

ai_use_lower_task_control.unit: percent of employees with less control over how to complete work

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published worker-reported generative-AI use, attitudes, education groups, and task-control groups; the report does not treat observed association as a causal effect.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not identify tool, task, intensity, employer policy, productivity, pay, displacement, or whether control caused adoption; subgroup categories and attitude items are not a worker-level panel.
observations.subgroup: Workers overall, by education, and by reported control over how work is completed.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI use may be higher where tasks fit the tool or employers permit it; lower use can reflect job type, privacy, quality concerns, or restricted access rather than lower capability.

observations.period: 2025 SHED; work location and schedule control

denominator.unit: published percentage base among workers or employees as specified

worked_from_home_any.unit: percent of workers in the prior week

worked_entirely_from_home.unit: percent of workers in the prior week

employer_needs_schedule_variation.unit: percent of employees with schedules varying based on employer needs

worker_requested_schedule_variation.unit: percent of employees with schedules varying at their own request

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published work-from-home and schedule-variation estimates; work location and schedule items describe separate dimensions of work organization.
observations.uncertainty: The measures do not identify commute time, hours, pay, schedule predictability, care outcomes, employer power, or whether a requested schedule change was granted.
observations.subgroup: Workers for work-location measures and employees for schedule-variation measures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Employer-driven schedule variation can be compatible with flexibility in some jobs, while a fixed schedule can still be difficult or inaccessible; neither measure alone ranks job quality.

related_sources.claim: BLS JOLTS supplies employer-based openings, hires, quits, and layoffs context with a different unit and denominator.
related_sources.access_boundary: Employer rates are not respondent-level job movement or AI exposure.

related_sources.claim: The NBER task-level generative-AI study supplies a complementary task/adoption surface.
related_sources.access_boundary: Task-level evidence and SHED worker perceptions are not interchangeable.

boundary: This record establishes 2025 respondent-level labor-market friction, mobility, work organization, and AI-use/control differences. It does not establish causal AI displacement, productivity, job quality, bargaining power, household welfare, political response, or a worker-level path from layoff or control to adoption and later exit. Employment, mobility, schedule, AI use, perceived benefit, and replacement concern remain separate stages.
